analysis.one_liner: Sets nationwide rights for people in HMOs and employer health plans: guaranteed appeals, outside review, and access to specialists and emergency care.
analysis.headline: Sen. Daschle introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights with 39 of 49 Senate Democrats as cosponsors, but the bill was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set federal standards for managed care plans and employer health coverage. It required plans to make coverage decisions on fixed deadlines, explain denials in plain language with the clinical reasons, and offer a fair internal appeal plus an independent outside appeal whose decision is binding. It also guaranteed access to emergency care without prior approval, direct access to OB-GYNs and pediatricians, standing referrals to specialists for chronic illness, exceptions to drug formularies when medically necessary, coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials, and the right to take some denied-care disputes to court. It applied these rules to group plans, group insurance, and individual coverage under three federal laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of Americans enrolled in HMOs and employer-sponsored health plans — the people whose care was subject to insurance company utilization review. Anyone whose plan denied a test, referral, drug, or hospital stay would get plain-language reasons, a fast internal appeal, and an independent outside review that the plan must obey, with fines for officials who ignore it. People with serious or chronic conditions would get direct access to OB-GYNs and pediatricians, standing specialist referrals, formulary exceptions, and coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in HMO and employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Plans must process coverage decisions on fixed deadlines (14 days for most prior authorizations, 72 hours for expedited cases) and a missed deadline counts as a denial the patient can appeal.
Denials must be explained in plain language with the clinical rationale, and patients get at least 180 days to request an internal review by someone who did not make the original denial.

Denials based on medical judgment can be appealed to an independent outside entity of at least three clinical peers; that decision is binding on the plan, and an official who refuses to authorize the benefit can owe the patient up to $1,000 a day until it is corrected.
Emergency services must be covered under the 'prudent layperson' standard without prior authorization, whether or not the provider is in-network, and without extra cost to the patient.

Patients may see a participating OB-GYN or pediatrician without a referral, and people with ongoing serious conditions can get standing referrals to specialists who can then coordinate and authorize their own care.

Plans with drug formularies must grant exceptions when a non-formulary drug is medically necessary, and cannot deny an FDA-approved drug or device as 'investigational' when the use is in the approved labeling.
People with life-threatening illnesses in approved clinical trials (funded by NIH, VA, or DoD) cannot be denied coverage of routine patient costs or discriminated against for participating.
The bill limits ERISA preemption so that some disputes over denied care by health insurance policyholders can proceed in court rather than being dismissed.
Utilization review programs cannot pay reviewers in ways that encourage denials of claims, must use qualified clinical staff, and must make reviewers reachable by phone.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care companies bear the compliance costs: staffed review programs, outside appeal contracts paid by the plan, benefit mandates, and fines for ignoring external review decisions. Employers that sponsor self-insured plans face the same standards and possible higher premiums. Enrollees who choose the new point-of-service option (out-of-network coverage) pay any added premium themselves. Critics of patients' rights bills generally argued that some of these costs would reach workers through premiums and that expanded court access raises liability exposure.

drawbacks.text: New review, appeal, and outside-review obligations are real compliance costs for health plans and self-insured employers, which would likely be reflected in premiums.

The bill lets plan officials who refuse to follow a binding external review be sued for up to $1,000 a day per patient and exposes them to cease-and-desist orders and additional civil penalties, expanding litigation risk.

The consumer choice option — the right to buy out-of-network point-of-service coverage — is paid for by the enrollee in added premiums and cost-sharing, so it is an option only for those who can afford it.
The bill regulates the terms of existing coverage only; it does nothing for the uninsured or for people priced out of coverage entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a genuine, then-widespread grievance: managed care plans denying or delaying care with little recourse, using reviewers paid in ways that could reward denials, shielded from suit by ERISA preemption. The core protections — fair appeals, binding outside review, emergency access without pre-approval, direct OB-GYN access — have since become standard practice, which supports the view that they were workable. The honest costs are insurer and employer compliance burdens, possible premium increases, and expanded litigation over denied care; the bill also left the uninsured untouched. On balance its benefits flowed to patients and its costs to plans and their sponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the Senate's first day and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress; it died in committee when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Daschle introduced S. 6 on January 22, 2001, the opening day of the 107th Congress, as the Democrats' Patients' Bill of Rights.
Thirty-nine of the Senate's 49 Democrats — a near-unanimous caucus — signed on as original cosponsors; no Republican appears on the cosponsor list.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral is the last recorded action on the bill: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the action history before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
The patients' rights issue stayed alive in that Congress through other vehicles and negotiation, but no federal patients' bill of rights became law in the 107th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans, and the employers that sponsor self-insured coverage, came out ahead: they avoided binding outside appeals, fines of up to $1,000 a day for ignoring review decisions, new access mandates, and expanded court access over denied care. Patients in managed care plans gained nothing from the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

against.what_they_did: Opposed patients' rights legislation that expanded patients' ability to sue health plans and pressed for sharply limited court access, which narrowed what any bill could pass.

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained lobbying campaign against patients' rights bills that imposed outside appeals, benefit mandates, and liability for denied care.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors were Senate Democrats — 39 of the caucus's 49 members — and no Republican cosponsored this bill, although the patients' rights issue overall drew some Republican support on other vehicles in that Congress.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans (HMOs)
industries.note: The bill subjects plan coverage decisions to uniform review standards, binding independent outside appeals paid for by the plan, fines up to $1,000 a day for ignoring those decisions, mandates for emergency and specialist access, and removal of the ERISA shield from certain denied-care lawsuits. Plans' savings from restrictive review came at patients' expense, so their interest in this bill ran against the people they covered.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring self-insured group health plans
industries.note: The patient-protection standards apply directly to ERISA group plans, creating compliance duties and possible premium pressure, though the same standards gave employees a fair appeal process that could reduce disputes.

The bill prohibits incentive arrangements that reward reviewers for denying care, bans interference with doctor-patient communications, protects patient advocates, and forbids discrimination against providers based on licensure — giving treating doctors standing in coverage disputes.
